tagline: Marsh views and former rice plantations along the road through Darien
intro: The Altamaha Historic Scenic Byway follows SR 99 and US 17 for 17 miles through McIntosh and Glynn counties and Darien. Marsh views, live oaks hung with Spanish moss and the Darien waterfront give the drive its coastal character. Georgia DOT lists Altamaha among its designated scenic byways, highlighting the coast’s cultural heritage and marsh ecosystems.

At Ridgeville, SR 99 is the Old Shell Road, with a historic community spread along both sides above the salt marshes. The Ridge preserves houses in Italianate, Greek Revival, Eastlake and Victorian Eclectic styles along that older road. Farther along the corridor, the marshes became ground for rice plantations: William Brailsford used enslaved African laborers to establish Hofwyl-Broadfield in the early 1800s. Rice growing there continued until 1913; the family then turned to dairying rather than sell the home.

Begin at the Sapelo Island Visitors Center and follow the byway toward Darien and Fort King George. The journey continues past Butler Island and Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation before reaching Needwood Church and School. At Hofwyl-Broadfield, remnants of rice levees survive beside the live oaks and dairy buildings. At the southern endpoint, Needwood’s one-room school served African-American students until the 1960s.
notice: Live oaks draped in Spanish moss line a corridor of marsh views.

moments.title: Fort King George
moments.text: The blockhouse at Fort King George is a reconstruction made with the help of old records and drawings. Scoutmen led by Colonel John Barnwell built the original cypress blockhouse, barracks and palisaded earthen fort in 1721. Until 1727, it served as the British Empire’s southernmost North American outpost. After its abandonment, James Oglethorpe brought Scottish Highlanders to the site in 1736. The museum covers the Guale Indians and the Santo Domingo de Talaje Mission. The museum also follows Darien’s later sawmilling industry, and remains of three sawmills are visible at the site.
moments.notice: The reconstructed fort includes a blockhouse, barracks, moat and palisades.

moments.title: Butler Island
moments.text: US 17 crosses the island’s eastern section on its connection to Darien. A 75-foot brick rice-mill chimney marks Butler Island’s plantation landscape. Fanny Kemble arrived with her husband, Pierce Mease Butler, in December 1838. She had been told that the people enslaved here were treated well and never sold; her diary recorded the mistreatment and living conditions she encountered. Kemble published her account as Journal of a Residence on a Georgian Plantation in 1838–1839. A later owner, Tillinghast L’Hommedieu Huston, converted the plantation into a dairy and lettuce farm. His 1927 house was destroyed by fire on June 26, 2024.
moments.notice: The rice mill’s brick chimney rises 75 feet.

moments.title: Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation
moments.text: Rice levees and remnants of a dairy operation share the grounds at Hofwyl-Broadfield. William Brailsford established the rice plantation in the early 1800s using enslaved African laborers to convert marshland along the Altamaha. The family continued growing rice until 1913, then started a dairy to avoid selling the home. Ophelia Dent left the plantation to Georgia in 1973. The state historic site’s nature trail follows the edge of the marsh where rice once grew; house tours show the furnishings and heirlooms Ophelia kept. A model in the museum shows the original estate.
moments.notice: Remnants of rice levees accompany moss-laden live oaks.
